concept.name: Heaps & Priority Queues

relationships.description: Dijkstra relies on a min-priority queue.
Top-K is a common coding pattern solved with heaps.

reviewRecord.reviewNotes: Seeded for SPEC-062 pillar coverage matrix.

spark.summary: A binary heap is a complete binary tree packed into a contiguous array that maintains the heap-order invariant in O(log n) per update and O(1) for min/max inspection.
spark.keyTakeaway: Packing a complete tree into a flat array gives O(log n) priority operations with L1-cache-friendly memory access, making binary and 4-ary heaps faster in practice than theoretically tighter pointer-based heaps.

concept.whyItMatters: Whenever a system needs the smallest or largest element from a changing stream—Dijkstra's shortest path, OS task schedulers, timer wheels, event-driven simulators, or top-k analytics—sorting the whole set on every insert ($O(n \log n)$) is prohibitively slow. A heap gives you $O(1)$ peek and $O(\log n)$ push/pop with zero pointer overhead.
whenToUse: Dynamic top-k / streaming quantiles: keeping the 100 largest elements across 100 million events using a size-k min-heap in $O(n \log k)$ time and $O(k)$ memory.
Graph shortest paths & MSTs (Dijkstra, Prim, A*): repeatedly popping the minimum-distance frontier vertex.
Multi-way external merge sort & LSM-tree compaction: merging k sorted SSTables or log files in $O(n \log k)$ time.
whenNotToUse: You need fast arbitrary search, range queries (`x <= k <= y`), or predecessor/successor lookups—use a balanced BST (B-tree, Red-Black tree) or skip list instead.
The dataset is static and queried once—`quickselect` finds the k-th element in $O(n)$ expected time without maintaining a heap.
Priorities are small bounded integers (e.g., 0–1023 ms timers)—a bucketed hierarchical timing wheel or radix heap gives $O(1)$ amortized operations.
keyPoints: Implicit array layout stores node `i`'s parent at `(i - 1) >> 1` and children at `2*i + 1` and `2*i + 2`, eliminating 16–24 bytes of left/right/parent pointers per node.
Floyd's bottom-up `heapify` builds a valid heap from an unsorted array in $O(n)$ time (not $O(n \log n)$), because half the nodes are leaves needing 0 swaps and most others sit near the bottom.

Standard heaps (`heapq` in Python, `PriorityQueue` in Java) do not support $O(\log n)$ arbitrary deletion or `decreaseKey`; you either maintain an external `pos[id]` index map (indexed heap) or push duplicate entries and skip stale pops (lazy deletion).

A $d$-ary heap (commonly $d = 4$) flattens tree height from $\log_2 n$ to $\log_4 n$ and aligns child scans within a single 64-byte CPU cache line, outperforming binary heaps on `decreaseKey`-heavy graph workloads.
Heaps are not stable by default: equal-priority items pop in arbitrary order unless you augment the key with a monotonic sequence counter `(priority, seq_id)`.

examples.title: Streaming Top-K heavy hitters in log aggregation
examples.scenario: An observability pipeline ingests 500,000 request-latency records per second and needs the 50 slowest endpoints over a 1-minute window (30M events) within a strict 10 MB memory budget.
examples.outcome: Using a fixed-capacity min-heap of size 50, each incoming event is compared against `heap[0]` in $O(1)$. Over 99.9% of events are smaller and discarded immediately; only larger ones trigger `heapreplace` in $O(\log 50) \approx 6$ comparisons, keeping memory under 4 KB.

examples.title: Lazy deletion vs. indexed heap in Dijkstra on road networks
examples.scenario: A routing engine computes shortest paths on a 20M-edge road graph where vertices are relaxed multiple times.
examples.outcome: With an indexed 4-ary heap (`pos[nodeId]`), `decreaseKey` updates the vertex in-place in $O(\log_4 V)$ without inflating heap size. When memory is plentiful, lazy deletion (pushing `(new_dist, node)` and ignoring pops where `dist > best_dist[node]`) avoids maintaining `pos[]` and is simpler to vectorize.

tradeOffs.pro: Indexed heaps keep heap size strictly $\le V$ and support true $O(\log n)$ `decreaseKey` and arbitrary removal.
tradeOffs.con: Requires a parallel `pos[id]` hash map or array updated on every swap, increasing constant-factor overhead and code complexity.

tradeOffs.pro: Cuts tree height in half (faster `siftUp` on `decreaseKey`) and fits 4 children into one 64-byte L1 cache line.
tradeOffs.con: `siftDown` during `pop` must compare $d$ children per level instead of 2, making `pop` slightly slower if comparisons are expensive (e.g., string keys).

tradeOffs.pro: Contiguous array layout gives predictable cache prefetching and 3–5x faster wall-clock time on real hardware.
tradeOffs.con: Fibonacci heaps offer $O(1)$ amortized `decreaseKey` theoretically, but pointer chasing causes L2/L3 cache misses and high memory overhead.

failureModes.name: Mutating priority keys in-place
failureModes.description: Code modifies an object's `priority` field after pushing it into `PriorityQueue` or `heapq`, silently corrupting the heap invariant so `pop()` returns non-minimum elements.
failureModes.mitigation: Treat heap keys as immutable; use an indexed heap `updateKey(id, newPriority)` method or push a new tuple and mark the old entry stale.

failureModes.name: Integer overflow in comparator subtraction
failureModes.description: A Java/C++ comparator written as `(a, b) -> a.score - b.score` overflows signed 32-bit `int` when comparing `INT_MIN` and positive numbers, flipping sort order.
failureModes.mitigation: Always use `Integer.compare(a.score, b.score)` or explicit `<` / `>` comparisons.

failureModes.name: Memory blowup with lazy deletion
failureModes.description: In dense graphs with frequent priority updates, lazy deletion leaves millions of stale entries inside the heap, degrading `pop()` to $O(\log E)$ and exhausting RAM.
failureModes.mitigation: Switch to an indexed heap when $|E| \gg |V|$, or compact/rebuild the heap in $O(n)$ whenever `stale_count > active_count`.

failureModes.name: Starvation from unstable priority ties
failureModes.description: Jobs with identical priority (e.g., `priority = 0`) are popped in heap-swap order rather than FIFO, starving older tasks.
failureModes.mitigation: Include a monotonic insertion counter `(priority, seq_id, payload)` so ties break deterministically in FIFO order.

commonMistakes: Building a heap by calling `heappush` $n$ times ($O(n \log n)$) instead of `heapify` ($O(n)$) when all elements are known upfront.
Calling `remove(obj)` on Java's `PriorityQueue` inside a hot loop without realizing it performs an $O(n)$ linear scan.
Using a max-heap when solving top-k largest elements instead of a size-k min-heap (which lets you discard small items in $O(1)$).
Confusing `heap[1..k]` in array order with sorted order—only `heap[0]` is guaranteed to be the extremum; reading the rest sorted requires $k$ pops.
Forgetting thread safety: `heapq` and `PriorityQueue` are not thread-safe; concurrent producers/consumers need a lock or `PriorityBlockingQueue`.

sections.content:
## The idea

A **binary heap** is a complete binary tree—every level is completely filled except possibly the last, which is filled from left to right—satisfying the **heap-order property**: in a min-heap, every parent's key is less than or equal to its children's keys (`A[parent(i)] <= A[i]`).

Because the tree is complete, it needs no node objects or pointers. Storing it level-by-level in a flat 0-indexed array maps tree navigation to cheap bit shifts: `parent(i) = (i - 1) >> 1`, `left(i) = (i << 1) + 1`, and `right(i) = (i << 1) + 2`. Every modification restores the invariant with one of two loops: **`siftUp`** (bubble a newly inserted or decreased key toward the root) or **`siftDown`** (sink a replaced root toward the leaves by swapping with its smaller child).

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace **Floyd's $O(n)$ `heapify`** followed by a `pop` on `[40, 10, 30, 50, 20, 5]`:

1. **Bottom-up `heapify`**: Start at the last non-leaf index `n // 2 - 1 = 2` (`30`) and `siftDown` backward to index `0`:
   - `i = 2` (`30`): child `5` (`5`) is smaller -> swap -> `[40, 10, 5, 50, 20, 30]`.
   - `i = 1` (`10`): children `50`, `20` are both `>= 10` -> no swap.
   - `i = 0` (`40`): smaller child is `i = 2` (`5`) -> swap `40` and `5` -> `[5, 10, 40, 50, 20, 30]`; continue sinking `40` at `i = 2` against child `i = 5` (`30`) -> swap -> **`[5, 10, 30, 50, 20, 40]`**.
2. **`popMin()`**:
   - Save `min = A[0]` (`5`). Move last element `A[5]` (`40`) to `A[0]` and shrink length to 5: `[40, 10, 30, 50, 20]`.
   - `siftDown(0)`: `40` compares children `10` and `30`, swaps with `10` -> `[10, 40, 30, 50, 20]`; at `i = 1`, `40` compares children `50` and `20`, swaps with `20` -> **`[10, 20, 30, 50, 40]`**.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Why Floyd's heapify is O(n) and d-ary heaps win on cache
sections.content:
## Why Floyd's heapify is O(n) and d-ary heaps win on cache

Building a heap by inserting $n$ items one by one takes $\sum_{i=1}^n \log i = \Theta(n \log n)$ in the worst case because each new item starts at the bottom and may `siftUp` to the root. **Floyd's `heapify`** flips the direction: it runs `siftDown` from `n/2 - 1` down to `0`. At height $h$, there are at most $\lceil n / 2^{h+1} \rceil$ nodes, and each sinks at most $h$ levels. Summing over all heights gives $n \sum_{h=1}^{\infty} h / 2^{h+1} = n$ comparisons—strictly $O(n)$.

In modern CPUs, pointer-heavy structures like Fibonacci heaps suffer L2/L3 cache misses (~10–60 ns per miss). A **4-ary heap** (`parent = (i - 1) >> 2`, `first_child = (i << 2) + 1`) packs all 4 children of a node into adjacent memory (16–32 bytes), fitting inside a single **64-byte L1 cache line**. It halves tree depth compared to a binary heap, cutting `decreaseKey` swaps by 50%.

## Priority queue implementation trade-offs

| Variant | `push` | `popMin` | `decreaseKey` | Memory / Cache |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Binary Heap** | $O(\log n)$ | $O(\log n)$ | $O(n)$ without index; $O(\log n)$ indexed | 1 contiguous array; best for general use |
| **4-ary Heap** | $O(\log_4 n)$ | $O(4 \log_4 n)$ | $O(\log_4 n)$ indexed | 4 children fit in 1 cache line; faster in Dijkstra |
| **Lazy-Delete Binary** | $O(\log E)$ | $O(\log E)$ amortized | $O(\log E)$ (push duplicate) | Simpler code; bloats to $O(E)$ entries |
| **Fibonacci Heap** | $O(1)$ | $O(\log n)$ amortized | $O(1)$ amortized | Heavy pointers; poor L1/L2 cache locality |
| **Balanced BST (TreeSet)** | $O(\log n)$ | $O(\log n)$ | $O(\log n)$ (remove + insert) | Supports range queries; ~3x higher RAM per node |

## Failure modes

- **Unbounded heap growth in streaming top-k**: Using a max-heap of size $n$ and calling `pop()` $k$ times wastes $O(n)$ memory; always invert the comparator to a fixed-size-$k$ min-heap so memory stays $O(k)$.
- **Non-transitive or NaN comparators**: Pushing IEEE-754 `NaN` floats into a heap breaks total ordering (`NaN < x` and `x < NaN` are both `false`), permanently trapping elements in wrong subtrees.
- **Stale index corruption in indexed heaps**: Forgetting to update `pos[id]` on *both* elements during a swap (or deleting an item from `pos` before swapping it to the end) causes out-of-bounds panics.
- **Comparator allocation pressure**: In Python (`heapq`), custom key functions aren't supported directly; wrapping every item in a new tuple or wrapper object on every push creates GC churn in tight loops.

sections.eyebrow: 06 / Practical variants: two-heap median & indexed timers
sections.content:
## Practical variants: two-heap median & indexed timers

Two-heap tracking maintains a **running median** in $O(\log n)$ per insert and $O(1)$ query: a max-heap stores the lower half of numbers and a min-heap stores the upper half, rebalancing whenever their sizes differ by more than 1.

For **system timers and schedulers** (e.g., Go's runtime network poller, which uses a **4-ary min-heap** for `time.Timer`), an indexed heap lets `timer.Reset()` or `timer.Stop()` adjust deadlines in $O(\log_4 n)$ without leaving expired timers clogging the queue.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Use `heapify` ($O(n)$) instead of repeated `push` ($O(n \log n)$) when initializing from a batch.
- [ ] For top-$k$ largest items, use a **min-heap** capped at size $k$ (and a max-heap for top-$k$ smallest).
- [ ] Add a monotonic sequence number `(priority, seq, item)` whenever equal-priority items require FIFO stability.
- [ ] Reject or sanitize `NaN` keys before insertion to preserve total ordering.
- [ ] Choose an indexed 4-ary heap over lazy deletion when `decreaseKey` frequency exceeds `pop` frequency (e.g., dense graphs or timer resets).

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Heap Priority Queue Algorithms

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: A binary heap is a complete binary tree packed into a contiguous array that maintains the heap-order invariant in O(log n) per update and O(1) for min/max inspection.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Contiguous Heap Array applies the primary invariant and coordinates with SiftUp / SiftDown Engine.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, SiftUp / SiftDown Engine experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Treat heap keys as immutable; use an indexed heap `updateKey(id, newPriority)` method or push a new tuple and mark the old entry stale.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Packing a complete tree into a flat array gives O(log n) priority operations with L1-cache-friendly memory access, making binary and 4-ary heaps faster in practice than theoretically tighter pointer-based heaps.
Avoid trap: Building a heap by calling `heappush` $n$ times ($O(n \log n)$) instead of `heapify` ($O(n)$) when all elements are known upfront.
Avoid trap: Calling `remove(obj)` on Java's `PriorityQueue` inside a hot loop without realizing it performs an $O(n)$ linear scan.
When to reach for it: Dynamic top-k / streaming quantiles: keeping the 100 largest elements across 100 million events using a size-k min-heap in $O(n \log k)$ time and $O(k)$ memory.
When to reach for it: Graph shortest paths & MSTs (Dijkstra, Prim, A*): repeatedly popping the minimum-distance frontier vertex.

putItTogether.title: Putting Heap Priority Queue Algorithms Together
putItTogether.summary: Packing a complete tree into a flat array gives O(log n) priority operations with L1-cache-friendly memory access, making binary and 4-ary heaps faster in practice than theoretically tighter pointer-based heaps.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Heap Priority Queue Algorithms before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Using a fixed-capacity min-heap of size 50, each incoming event is compared against `heap[0]` in $O(1)$. Over 99.9% of events are smaller and discarded immediately; only larger ones trigger `heapreplace` in $O(\log 50) \approx 6$ comparisons, keeping memory under 4 KB.
